newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Red Cross to put Zaire refugee office in Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross to put Zaire refugee office in Kisangani.

text.p: The International Committee of the Red Cross said on Monday it would open an office in Kisangani to reach Hutu refugees trapped in remote corners of eastern Zaire after fleeing a Tutsi revolt there.

With the scale of the problem still unclear, Roman Catholic Church sources said that 50 displaced Zaireans had arrived in the northeastern town of 500,000 people in poor condition and had been taken to hospitals.
Unconfirmed estimates suggest that hundreds of similar cases may have already reached the town and dispersed among the population.

"When the needs become known and the security situation improves we will be able to respond with specialist help. For now this is the only possible route for providing assistance," ICRC spokesman Andreas Fuog told Reuters.
Kisangani is the last outpost of tenuous Zairean authority before tens of thousands of square kms (miles) of forest and hills.
Thousands of displaced Zaireans and Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees are believed to have left Bukavu and Goma, now in rebel hands, heading west into the forest wilderness.
But information from the region has come only from the handful who have made it is far as Kisangani and through occasional contacts with missionary radio.
"We don't know exactly how many people there are but it is likely the majority are not on the main road but on forest trails because of the insecurity," said Fuog.
The charity Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF-Doctors without Frontiers) has also sent an exploratory mission to Kisangani.
The main road from Goma and Bukavu to Kisangani was used as a line of retreat for troops from the battlefront.
Flights over the area revealed few people on the road, but also that the villages were deserted.
"As the soldiers pass through they look for food, so the villagers spend the day under the trees," said Kisangani Governor Lombeya Bosongo.

Kisangani was quiet on Monday and there was little shooting on Sunday night, after the local military commander warned troops who had pulled back to Kisangani that if they carried weapons on the street they would be shot.
Drunk and ill-disciplined soldiers from the battle front hundreds of kms (miles) away subjected the town to two nights of shooting and sporadic looting on Friday and Saturday.
Lombeya said soldiers had begun returning down the road towards their abandoned positions. This could not be independently confirmed.
A convoy from the Kisangani Chamber of Commerce on Sunday set off along the road to the east to help anyone it could find.
